primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Congenital chloride diarrhea due to SLC26A3 deficiency
mechanism: Loss of the intestinal SLC26A3 chloride-bicarbonate exchanger impairs chloride absorption and bicarbonate secretion in ileum/colon, causing chloride-rich watery diarrhea, extracellular-volume depletion, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
vignette: A newborn has abdominal distention and profuse watery diarrhea beginning shortly after birth. The pregnancy was complicated by polyhydramnios. Laboratory studies show hypochloremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Urinary chloride is low, whereas stool chloride is markedly elevated.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractors: Secretory diarrhea from a VIP-secreting tumor
distractor_notes: Neonatal Bartter syndrome causes renal salt wasting with elevated urinary chloride; this infant instead has chloride-rich diarrhea and low urinary chloride.
Microvillus inclusion disease causes severe congenital diarrhea but does not characteristically produce the specific chloride-rich stool with hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis caused by SLC26A3 loss.
Congenital sodium diarrhea is a distinct intestinal transport disorder; the hallmark here is excessive fecal chloride loss from defective chloride-bicarbonate exchange.

VIP-mediated secretory diarrhea is not the typical congenital presentation and classically causes bicarbonate-rich losses with metabolic acidosis rather than the characteristic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
key_expl: Congenital chloride diarrhea is caused by biallelic SLC26A3 defects. Loss of the intestinal Cl−/HCO3− exchanger causes chloride-rich watery diarrhea from birth. The resulting volume and chloride depletion produces hypochloremic, often hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; high stool chloride distinguishes the disorder from renal chloride-wasting states.
objective: Recognize congenital chloride diarrhea from neonatal chloride-rich watery diarrhea, low urinary chloride, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
